entry.content:
Before writing this, I glanced at the build machine: 5 tmux sessions running, 372 task directories under ~/.local/state/ai-jobs totaling 3.1 GB, load average 2.90 and drifting between two and seven the whole time. The machine has 128 cores, up for four and a half days. Those numbers are a single sampled instant—they’d changed again by the time I finished this paragraph, which is itself part of the point.

The projects on hand at the same moment: a Rust + SQL site reworking its statistics query, a Next.js app retiring its service worker, a Bun + Hono service fixing a tunnel origin, a Prisma + tRPC monorepo, a C# game private server filling in data fields, a C/C++ SDL3/WASM port, and two Zola/Hexo documentation sites. 64 directories and 36 git repositories under ~/Code.

This isn’t the “I have a lot of windows open” kind of parallelism. Anyone can open windows; the hard part is making progress on all of them at once without contaminating each other.

First, why it’s even worth it

With a single project, the most expensive part of AI collaboration is waiting: ten minutes for a full test run, five for a build, however long for browser regression. During that time the only things a person can do are sit there or switch to something else—and switching back means reloading context.

The first payoff of running eight projects in parallel is exactly this: the waiting gets filled by other lines. A’s build is running while B’s failure log just comes back; C waits on a human confirmation while D’s tests go red and need fixing. The machine’s throughput gets pulled up, and the human brain no longer has idle gaps.

The second payoff is reusing a solution from one line on another. Today, figuring out in av-site that “creating an index must stay inside the same transaction block as acquiring the lock” naturally led to thinking about “the deletion order when retiring a worker” in AstroDX—both are cases of “nothing can slip in between the two steps.” That kind of cross-project intuition only happens when you have several lines in hand at once.

But the payoff has preconditions, and here they are.

Rules must be layered, not copied

~/.agents/AGENTS.md is the single source of truth; ~/.codex/AGENTS.md and ~/.dsh/AGENTS.md are symlinks to it, and ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md references it via @. To change a rule you only change that one copy—three copies will inevitably drift.

The source of truth holds only what’s universal across projects: hold conversations in Chinese, Conventional Commits, the local machine isn’t the build machine, which machine to go to remotely, how to persist tasks over 30 seconds, where the proxy is.

Project-level AGENTS.md files only describe what’s unique to that project, and some really do write them narrowly:

  • av-site/AGENTS.md: all five CI steps green is the prerequisite for merging; changing OpenAPI types requires bun run gen:client; how to spin up a temporary postgres for database tests with #[ignore]; curl from the build machine needs a UA or Cloudflare returns 403; add SET default_transaction_read_only = on; before production troubleshooting.
  • eagler-touhou-next/AGENTS.md: this Mac is read/write and Git only; which checkout directory on the build machine; bun is pinned to 1.4.2; where the project’s own postgres:18 container lives.
  • th15/AGENTS.md is only 15 lines: the ownership of two trees.

That middle category—“which machine is the build machine”—is actually written in both files. It looks redundant, but the division of labor differs: the source of truth says “there is a build machine, pick by priority,” while the project file says “this project is fixed to this one, the checkout directory is here.” The former is a rule, the latter a fact.

There’s one more hard rule: every project must be able to state clearly “where it runs”—if you can’t write it down, the project isn’t ready to be parallelized yet.

Tasks must have an identity

Something run remotely can’t just be a ssh host 'bun run build' and done with it—drop the SSH and it’s gone, and reconnecting doesn’t tell you where it got to.

The rule in the source of truth, “remote SSH task persistence and reconnection recovery,” specifies this (shared by all projects):

Each task gets an independent ID, an independent tmux session, and an independent ~/.local/state/ai-jobs/<任务ID>/ directory. Inside the directory, run.sh begins with set -uo pipefail, umask 077, exec > output.log, trap writing the exit code into a file, echo $$ > pid, date -Is > started, then explicitly exporting PATH and HTTP(S)_PROXY.

Startup, logs, exit code, process ID, and start time are all five on disk. If SSH drops, go back by the original ID and read the status—do not resubmit. If the tmux session is gone but there’s also no exit code, the status counts as unknown: keep cross-checking the process and artifacts, and don’t treat it as success or as failure.

What’s forbidden is sharing a fixed ai-task session—several lines firing send-keys into the same session amounts to throwing commands into a shell you don’t recognize.

Recent tasks’ exit codes include both 0 and 1 (adjust-download-policy-red is 1, adjust-prod-cold is 1, a batch of adjust-consent mixed 1/0). Parallelism isn’t eight lines all green—it’s eight lines’ results each landing on disk, each queryable, with the red ones not dragging the others down.

Write to one place at a time

Two lines editing the same file at once is the number-one incident source in this workflow.

The unit of dispatch isn’t the project, it’s the file. Today the write-sets of the four lines are: av-site/infra/migrations/*, AstroDX/apps/web/public + src/lib, acgn-flow/src/server/*, drama-site/apps/web/src/*. The four groups are mutually disjoint.
(This is part 1 of 2 of the same post.)

Conversely, if the same package.json or root tsconfig needs to be changed, make them sequentially dependent: finish one before starting the next. Hard parallelism here only produces git conflicts and edits that overwrite each other.

When shared configuration must be changed across projects, I’d rather pause the line I’m on and wait for it to land.

Verification is tiered by scope of change

What most easily slackens under parallelism is verification, because every line wants to wrap up quickly.

The rule is tier by change, not by how much time is free:

  • One file changed → lint just that file, run just that test file; it can be done locally.
  • Cross-module change → go up to the build machine and run the whole-repo check for that project (AstroDX’s scripts/remote/verify.sh runs 739 tests + lints 719 files).
  • Anything with side effects (migrations, deployments, data fixes) → add real-device acceptance; for example, av-site changes to playback must run check-live-playback.py with a rate-limit round, and all-green smoke isn’t enough.

The only valid reason to downgrade verification is “this change isn’t worth that cost,” never “I’m busy right now.” Being busy is precisely what parallelism creates; trading busyness for cheap verification just pays back the time parallelism saved.

The costs, recorded in plain sight

The above is method; below is the ledger.

Context dilutes itself. With eight lines in hand, the memory of each grows thin. So the moment a line lands, “why it was changed this way” must go straight into a code comment or that project’s docs—don’t count on remembering next time. Of the 86 lines in 0055's migration file, 52 are comments, and AstroDX’s docs/verification/service-worker-retirement-2026-10-30.md even records when the script itself went wrong—both for this reason.

Review is the bottleneck, and it doesn’t scale with parallelism. Eight lines each produce output, and the merge decision all lands on one person. So better to let the AI go slower and produce less than to have it change 20 files at once—a giant change that can’t be decomposed takes longer to read through than to do yourself.

Build-machine resources are shared. A load average of two to seven looks low, but that’s headroom on 128 cores; at the same moment, two or three of several tmux sessions are running browser regressions and competing for memory. Lines running full test suites need to be scheduled on idle cores; single-core cases like taskset -c 0 get slowed by other lines, and timing issues on a slow CPU only surface under that condition—which is both a blessing and a trap.

Task directories grow if not cleaned. 372 directories, 3.1 GB, four and a half days of uptime. After a run, --keep keeps the evidence, and it should be swept a week later; it hasn’t been swept yet, which already counts as debt.

One more thing often overlooked: parallelism makes “done” cheap. One line goes red and nobody cares; another goes green and keeps moving, and the red one gets buried. So at the end of each day, look through the directories with non-zero exit codes, not at “how many were delivered today.”

Who this suits

Who it doesn’t suit: people whose changes are strongly linear, who can only think about one thing at a time, who dislike writing rule files.

There’s only one prerequisite for it to suit you: the project must already be verifiable in a remote form. A build machine, a verify script, and “where to run it” written into files—with all three in place you can split lines; missing any one, and raising parallelism only moves “stuck” from local to remote.

As for the AI’s side, it neither knows nor cares that other lines are running. It’s kept apart by the “don’t touch that directory” constraints in rule files, by the identity of task directories, by disjoint write sets. All these partitions are built in advance by a human; the AI just runs inside them.

When eight lines run at once, what I’m actually doing is quite boring: reading exit codes, watching logs, judging which line should continue and which should stop, writing the reasons into files. The real parallelism happens on disk and CPU; the human part remains serial—except what’s serialized is judgment, not typing.

(This is part 2 of 2 of the same post.)
entry.summary: Using AI to maintain a bunch of projects with completely different tech stacks in parallel: how rules are layered, how tasks are isolated, and where the costs are recorded
entry.title: What I'm Doing When Eight Tracks Run in Parallel

entry.content:
2aa1194ed, titled “Merge latest main into zsf”. A completely ordinary merge commit.

It deleted the entire Adjust runtime. Under packages/api/src/adjust/, 7 of the 8 files were deleted outright, and diff --stat was 4 insertions and 292 deletions.

No conflicts. No compile errors. CI was green.

How the deletion slipped in

The merge’s two parents are e5051db93 and 93173a00b (main), and the merge base is e11e286ff. On the base, these 8 files were intact, and all the git ls-tree references were present.

The problem was that the zsf line had already deleted them: that line was meant to implement a different feature, and from its perspective Adjust was “something extra that existed on main,” so removing it made the local tree cleaner. When merging, git therefore faced “deleted on one side, untouched on the other”—under the three-way merge rules, the deletion counts as zsf’s change and is kept as-is.

This is not a revert, nor is it a conflict. A conflict at least stops and asks you. This kind of merge takes effect silently, and the commit message only says “Merge latest main.”

Even more conveniently, there were no compile errors after the deletion. That’s because in the same batch of commits, all references to import "@nq/api/adjust", adjust-tracking, and adjust-session were deleted along with it—otherwise, with the references still present and the implementation gone, pnpm typecheck would have gone red.

So the whole set of green lights—“tests green, typecheck green, build green”—was completely useless here. They check whether it compiles, not whether the feature is still there.

How it was found

A single command:

git grep '@nq/api/adjust' upstream/preview

Zero hits.

That was the lesson, short enough to serve as a mantra: After merging across major branches, don’t just look at typecheck—grep for the feature name. If a few more people merge after 2aa1194ed, this clue will be completely buried—the feature name is still in the docs, but the window in the minds of people who remember it is only a few days.

After it was found, 88cdad163 restored the runtime with 86 files and 6,117 insertions, filling in A2/A3/A4/A6/A7 all at once. As of 10-23, the audit document 09-adjust-audit.md still concluded “0%—there is no Adjust integration anywhere in the repository.”

Restoring it was only half the battle; the next part was where the real thinking began.

8 Event Tokens are not 8 events

The vendor provided 8 Event Tokens, operations had already created them in the dashboard, and they required first purchase and refunds to carry amounts. The easiest implementation would be “send whenever you see a Token”—8 if statements.

But events are not equal. Split by “who is the single source of truth,” they fall into two categories from the start:

EventLaneRevenue
registrationSDK (native)No
first_purchaseS2SYes
purchaseS2SYes
refundS2SYes (refund amount)
first_unlockS2SNo
episode_unlockS2SNo
vip_activationS2SNo
vip_expiredS2SNo

So the first thing the enqueueing code does is split the sets:

/** 带收入的事件 —— 入队时必须拿到合法金额与币种，否则落 BLOCKED 而不是发一条 0 元收入。 */export const ADJUST_REVENUE_EVENTS: ReadonlySet<string> = new Set(  ADJUST_INTERNAL_EVENTS.filter(e => e.revenue).map(e => e.key),);

After the split, there are several rules hardcoded in the code and impossible to change from the dashboard.

One payment can only be recorded once. When first purchase matches, send only first_purchase and no longer send purchase:

function mappingCandidates(internalEvent: string, firstPurchase: boolean): string[] {  if (!ADJUST_REVENUE_EVENTS.has(internalEvent)) return [internalEvent];  const chain = internalEvent === "PURCHASE" || internalEvent === "FIRST_PURCHASE"    ? ["PURCHASE"]    : [internalEvent, "PURCHASE"];  return firstPurchase ? ["FIRST_PURCHASE", ...chain] : chain;}

The candidate order puts specific events before generic ones, and stops at the first match. When FIRST_PURCHASE is not configured, it naturally falls back to the type event or PURCHASE, and the whole chain doesn’t break just because one line is missing in the dashboard.

Non-revenue events have no fallback. Note that the first line above directly returns [internalEvent]. If EPISODE_UNLOCK lacks a mapping, it falls to BLOCKED / MISSING_S2S_MAPPING and does not fall back to PURCHASE—if it did, it would pointlessly record a 0-yuan revenue entry, creating a bunch of gaps in reports that are harder to trace than a missing entry.

Unlocks do not double-count revenue. Coins are bought in advance on top-up orders; unlocking merely spends them. Therefore, the revenue for first_unlock / episode_unlock is always empty.

Membership activation and revenue are two events from the same order. Both vip_activation and purchase are generated by the same order, so the unique key of the delivery row is expanded from (order_id, environment) to (order_id, environment, internal_event). currency is also made nullable at the same time—stuffing the string "INVALID" into non-revenue events would get rejected by the vendor’s currency validation.

Every missing piece must be visible. If any link in the chain is unsatisfied—no identity, environment mismatch, missing mapping, missing S2S token, invalid amount—write a BLOCKED row with a reason code; do not silently drop it. Black holes like “configured but no identity” must be visible in the dashboard’s postback records; otherwise you’ll forever be saying, “It should have been sent.”

The callback side

GET|POST /api/webhooks/adjust/callback. Map status codes to their retry rules: 200 accepted or already received, 400 this one’s dead, don’t resend, 401 auth failed, 404 not paired yet, 503 our side had a temporary failure.

Auth nonce on both sides timingSafeEqual; the idempotency key is a hash of created_at; the receipt is pinned only on the first attempt (where callbackAt: null).

Once this was running, I ran into two vendor behaviors, both of which made it into code comments and tests:

  • 2xx comes in three shapes: {"status":"OK"}, an empty body {}, and an empty string. The original check only recognized the first, so the other two were treated as UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN doesn’t retry automatically — a payment already recorded on the vendor side would never reconcile. Changed it so any 2xx counts as SENT.
  • {order_id} is not a placeholder. It isn’t in the 262-entry placeholder table behind help.adjust.com, so writing it into the callback URL leaves it unreplaced and the other side receives the literal text. But the S2S callback_params appends the real value to the end of the URL, so the same key shows up twice, literal first, and first() always picks up {order_id}. The parser now walks getAll and skips {...}-shaped segments.

After the second fix I deliberately re-verified the worst case: reverted the template to the old form with {order_id}, created a transaction and ran it end to end, and the receipt got pinned as usual. Only after confirming that production was running the new parser — and not just “the template happened to be clean” — did I feel safe shipping it.

Two gates, deliberately different

AD_REAL_SENDING_ENABLED=0 guards Meta CAPI and TikTok — neither has a sandbox, so a preview sends something that’s really recorded in the ad account. Adjust is therefore unaffected: it has a real sandbox, and adjustEnvironment() maps previews to SANDBOX.

To silence Adjust previews too, use the other gate, ADJUST_S2S_ENABLED=0.

The gates are separate because the reasons differ. One is “don’t pollute the real account”; the other is “this pipeline shuts itself up.” Merge them into one, and later, when you only want to silence one side, you’ll have to rewrite it.

Wrapping up

Production is a separate a2bcb4351, based on release-v1.2.45, containing only what was verified on preview — no Mock/Kafka scaffolding and no consent modal.

In hindsight, the cost of a merge accident like 2aa1194ed isn’t in “getting it back” — from the merge (10-27 10:41 UTC+7) to the recovery commit 88cdad163 (same day, 19:47 UTC+8) was eight hours, and not a single line was lost from git. The cost is in those eight hours: the feature was assumed to “already exist,” nobody touched it, and regression tests can’t cover a module that doesn’t exist.

The cheapest line of defense is turning grep into a fixed post-merge step. Typecheck answers “does it compile”; only grep answers “is it still there.”
entry.summary: A merge with no conflicts and no errors wiped out 292 lines of ad-attribution runtime in one go, and only a single line of grep caught it; also jotting down the rules settled on when splitting 8 events into separate lanes
entry.title: The Typecheck Was Green After the Merge

entry.content:
The site is written in Bun + Hono, runs in a container, and is exposed via Cloudflare Tunnel. Five days ago there were two bugs in a row (be15f5a, 2ea4f53, eight minutes apart), both of which “brought local development assumptions into this topology.”

First: origin is http

When the tunnel sends requests in from the public internet, the hop to the container is http. So anywhere that gets the origin via request.url gets http://....

Most places don’t care; two do:

  • the cookie’s Secure attribute, and OAuth callback URL construction—the callback comes out as http, but the browser treats the return as https, so they don’t match.
  • generating absolute URLs for external use (share links, links in emails)—what goes out is http, and when users click it they either get redirected or it simply doesn’t work.

Cloudflare includes x-forwarded-host and x-forwarded-proto. So should we restore based on those?

No. x-forwarded-host is a header the client can forge, and when connecting directly to the container port, it’s entirely determined by the requester. Trusting it unconditionally opens another hole for changing the origin.

I wrote a publicRequest(request, configuredUrl) (src/server/public-request.ts, 10 lines total), with these rules:

  1. If no public domain is configured, return it as-is.
  2. If the request host doesn’t match the configured host → leave it alone. That means it came in through another entry point (loopback preview, direct intranet connection), and that origin belongs to the user; changing it would actually be wrong.
  3. If the hosts match but the protocol is already the same → leave it alone. Don’t copy the request for no reason.
  4. The only remaining case: hosts match, protocols differ → change only the protocol and rebuild it with new Request().
const configured = new URL(configuredUrl);const incoming = new URL(request.url);if (incoming.host !== configured.host || incoming.protocol === configured.protocol)  return request;incoming.protocol = configured.protocol;return new Request(incoming, request);

new Request(url, request) preserves the method, body, headers, and all other properties, replacing only the origin. In src/server/index.ts, change fetch: app.fetch to go through this handling before forwarding:

fetch: (...[request, bindings, executionCtx]: Parameters<typeof app.fetch>) =>  app.fetch(publicRequest(request, process.env.APP_URL), bindings, executionCtx),

This way, “restoring https” only happens when it’s confirmed to be this entry point, and a forged x-forwarded-host is ignored because the host doesn’t match.

The three tests/public-request.test.ts cases cover exactly this: restoring https while keeping the POST body / cookies / query string all intact; not trusting x-forwarded-host: af.saop.cc when the actual connection is 127.0.0.1:31270; and returning the same object (rather than a copy) when the protocol is the same or no public domain is configured.

Strictly speaking, the third isn’t a security requirement but predictability—if you’re debugging locally with curl 127.0.0.1:3000 and suddenly see an https-style origin, you’d be suspicious for a long time.

Second: the container’s 127.0.0.1 is not the host’s

For the container to access the internet, it has to go through the proxy 127.0.0.1:11090 on the host machine.

In compose.yaml it’s written like this:

environment:  HTTP_PROXY: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}  HTTPS_PROXY: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}  NO_PROXY: ${OUTBOUND_NO_PROXY:-}  http_proxy: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}  https_proxy: ${OUTBOUND_PROXY:-}  no_proxy: ${OUTBOUND_NO_PROXY:-}

Both cases are written because Bun/undici recognizes lowercase, while many shell tools only recognize uppercase.

One pitfall has to be stated clearly right in .env.production.example:

# 宿主机上的代理，不是容器自己的 127.0.0.1OUTBOUND_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:11090OUTBOUND_NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,postgres,redis

OUTBOUND_PROXY is set to 127.0.0.1, which points to the host’s loopback. But 127.0.0.1 inside the container is the container itself; if it doesn’t match, nothing on the network works. At the same time, NO_PROXY must include service names like postgres and redis—they’re on the same compose network, so connecting directly is faster than going through the proxy, and it also prevents the proxy from not recognizing those names.

Don’t bake it into the image

The proxy is environment-specific: it exists on the build machine, may not exist on a laptop, and may use a different port in production. So inject it only at runtime via environment, and don’t write a single ENV HTTP_PROXY in Dockerfile.

If you bake it into the image, the image is tied to the network configuration at build time. Moreover, ENV in Dockerfile overrides runtime injection—you’d have to rebuild the image to change it, even though it’s clearly a configuration issue.

What the two have in common

Both bugs have the same shape: the code was written assuming “requests connect directly, network connects directly,” but the deployment topology isn’t like that.

The tunnel and the container each work fine on their own; what’s missing is a layer of translation at their boundary—one translates the inbound origin from http back to https (and only when it should), and the other translates the outbound target from the container loopback to the host loopback.

Things at this kind of boundary have a characteristic: everything works locally, because locally it is both the “public entry point” and the “host machine,” so both assumptions hold at once. It only blows up after deployment, and the blow-up happens far from the change.

deploy/README.md now has explanations for both sections, placed together. Next time someone adds a new environment variable, they’ll at least see the sentence “the container and the host are two different loopbacks.”
entry.summary: After the reverse proxy comes in, the origin becomes HTTP, and there's no host proxy inside the container; both are solved by runtime configuration
entry.title: The server behind the tunnel thinks it's in HTTP

entry.content:
88b54539 refactor(web): retire service worker caching safely, 1107 lines deleted and 354 lines added. The numbers make it look like a refactor, but really it’s arranging an exit for something that’s still alive.

Why I Wanted to Delete It

This site is a Next.js app, and PWA precaching used to be handled by Serwist. The problems gradually surfaced:

  • After a deploy, the precache in the browser is still there, so users get the previous version of the HTML and the previous version of the JS.
  • Once the old chunks in the cache get purged, pages that reference them just go blank.
  • When something goes wrong, the only fix is for users to “clear the cache” on their end; we have no remedy at all.

And the benefits keep shrinking: the app already installs normally (on 2026-10-30 I specifically checked Google’s current installability criteria — a service worker hasn’t been required for a long time), and we aren’t using push either. All that’s left is “open it offline,” and the price is version mismatch.

The conclusion: retire the caching layer.

But You Can’t Just Delete the Registration

The most intuitive approach is to put navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistrations() in the page and then unregister() them one by one.

Not enough. unregister() only stops it from taking over new navigations; the already-running worker is still alive and still feeding requests to the cache on fetch events. The user’s current visit is still the old version. And once the registrations are deleted, nobody is in charge of those Cache Storage entries anymore — they’ll occupy space forever.

Nor can we just brute-force it with Clear-Site-Data: that would wipe IndexedDB and cookies along with everything else, and we still have local data.

What’s needed is a retirement worker: still published at the old /sw.js URL, dedicated to cleaning up after itself.

What the Retirement Worker Looks Like

apps/web/public/sw.js is 52 lines in total, with no fetch handler — that’s the key point: as soon as the new worker installs, requests no longer go through the cache.

const legacyCaches = new Set([  "next-static", "rsc-payloads", "catalog-manifests", "cover-images",  "static-images", "fonts", "pages", "astrodx-shell-state",  `serwist-precache-v2-${self.registration.scope}`,]);function retire() {  if (!cleanup) {    cleanup = (async () => {      await self.clients.claim();      const names = await caches.keys();      const results = await Promise.allSettled(        names.filter((n) => legacyCaches.has(n)).map((n) => caches.delete(n)),      );      if (results.some((r) => r.status === "rejected")) return;      await self.registration.unregister();    })().catch(() => {}).finally(() => { cleanup = undefined; });  }  return cleanup;}self.addEventListener("install", (e) => e.waitUntil(self.skipWaiting()));self.addEventListener("activate", (e) => e.waitUntil(retire()));self.addEventListener("message", (e) => {  if (e.data?.type === "astrodx-retire-service-worker") e.waitUntil(retire());});

A few deliberate choices:

skipWaiting as soon as it’s installed. No waiting, no waiting for the old worker to step aside. There’s no version-compatibility issue here — the new worker caches nothing, so the sooner it takes over, the better.

clients.claim() first, then delete. Take over the current page so that while caches are being deleted, the page isn’t simultaneously having things pulled from those caches by the old worker. The cleanup has to actually finish before unregister(): if even one entry in Promise.allSettled rejects, return and stay in the passive state until next time. Unregistering without a clean delete would leave behind a pile of unmanaged cache directories.

The cleanup variable is there to prevent re-entrancy. activate and message can arrive almost simultaneously; without a lock, caches.delete runs twice.

Only delete from a whitelist. Other libraries or experiments may have put things in Cache Storage; wiping everything with caches.keys() would be overstepping. The nine names were copied from Serwist’s generated output, and the one with a scope has to be assembled from a runtime value.

No fetch handler. That’s the definition of “retirement.” With a handler it’s still intercepting, and version mismatch is still possible.

Who Triggers the Update

The retirement worker sits at /sw.js, but not everyone will automatically go and fetch it.

The browser only checks whether sw.js has changed when navigating to a page within the scope. A user who stays put on the current tab will never discover the new version. So we need a client-side driver:

export async function retireLegacyServiceWorkers(host, origin: string) {  const scope = new URL("/", origin).href;  const script = new URL("sw.js", scope).href;  const registrations = await host.getRegistrations();  await Promise.all(registrations.map(async (registration) => {    const latest = registration.installing ?? registration.waiting ?? registration.active;    if (registration.scope !== scope || latest?.scriptURL !== script) return;    try { await registration.update(); } catch { /* 离线，下次 */ }    registration.active?.postMessage?.({ type: "astrodx-retire-service-worker" });  }));}

The outer try/catch catches two cases: getRegistrations() may be rejected by storage policy, and the registration may be concurrently unregistered while it’s being processed. This component only needs to give it a poke; no exception may ever break the page.

components/site/service-worker-retirement.tsx only calls it in production, when readyState is complete or load, and when online.

Only update(), never register(). New visitors have no SW to begin with, so registering an empty one just to have it unregister itself is pointless busywork; only existing registrations are worth poking. Two matching conditions are enforced: the scope must be the site root, and the newest worker’s scriptURL must be exactly /sw.js — other paths may host third-party workers, and touching those is none of our business. To find the newest worker, use installing ?? waiting ?? active; looking only at active returns null at the very moment when “a new worker is installing,” which is precisely the object we need to handle.

The message listener covers this case: update() installed a new worker, but the page didn’t navigate again, so the new worker never fired activate. Just postMessage to get it working without waiting for the user to refresh. This message also handles retries — if the worker in the passive state failed to clean up last time, it gets another push on the next visit.

Tests First

Write the tests first, watch them go red first. In the end there were 9: 6 testing the page-side logic, 3 testing the worker itself.

The 6 page-side guards: new visitors don’t register; only the worker at this site’s root path is updated (other scripts, other scopes, other origins are left alone); registrations taken over by a third-party worker are untouched; a first install that is installed but not yet activated is handled; an offline failure doesn’t blow up the page and the next call retries; a rejected getRegistrations() is a silent no-op.

The 3 worker-side tests use node:vm to run sw.js in a bare shell with no IndexedDB / localStorage / OPFS / navigation API — any code that casually wipes user data or forces a refresh blows up on the spot. Three cases: normal retirement (assert no fetch listener, claim happens before deletion, the last step is unregister, only the three non-allowlisted caches remain); deletion failure leaves it in passive and the message can be retried; unrelated messages don’t trigger anything.

One point is especially worth writing about: don’t clear outside the allowlist. I understood why this matters better after it went red — if caches.keys() were deleted unconditionally, then someday someone puts something in Cache Storage, and the retired worker would delete it on the very day it ships, by which time the person opening that file is someone else entirely.

Verification

Remote scripts/remote/verify.sh --keep: 719 files pass lint, 739 tests all green.

The real acceptance test was in Chromium 156: simulate an old user with old caches installed, run five rounds of migration, and check each round whether the registration disappears and the 9 cache names are emptied. All five rounds passed, and the two old tabs never refreshed the whole time.

Two rounds had problems with the script itself, neither of them product issues:

  • The first version of the script started from about:blank, and the moment it visited sessionStorage it was rejected (no origin).
  • The later diagnostic script had a sampling race — it read state in the same frame the worker was doing its work, reading faster than the work happened, so it saw intermediate states.

The second fix was to the script, not the product: wait until both conditions — “registration is empty and the staging cache is cleared” — hold simultaneously before deciding, instead of a fixed sleep followed by a glance. Using sleep to paper over the timing just turns the test into a probability problem.

What’s left behind

The file public/sw.js will stay for the long haul. As long as old registrations are still sitting in some old users’ browsers, it’s useful; new visitors’ browsers will fetch it, install it, run it, unregister, and stay clean. Only when the share of old registrations in traffic approaches zero can the file be deleted too — though keeping it costs nothing, a 52-line file with no handlers.

The easiest thing to get backwards in this whole process is the order: deleting caches before claiming, or unregistering even when deletion fails. The former makes pages that are currently open break while the caches are being deleted; the latter leaves garbage behind. Both are “looks like it works too” mistakes, and only tests and acceptance criteria can pin them down.
entry.summary: A Service Worker still running old caches can neither be deleted directly nor kept; a record of a retirement process involving 1,107 deleted lines.
entry.title: Letting Service Worker Step Down on Its Own

entry.content:
The detail page for channel stats takes 1.5 seconds. On a backend dashboard that’s not a disaster, but waiting a second and a half on every refresh is something users remember.

The baseline is a production scale of 246,000 clicks over a 30-day window. The detail page takes 1.51 s, the cross-channel overview 1.49 s, and the share page 0.85 s—the share page is shown to advertisers, and a second and a half of white screen looks bad.

The problem isn’t data volume

First, let’s clarify the term “valid device”: among distinct devices, those that actually landed within 30 minutes of the click. The criterion is a macro called LANDED, whose core is a single EXISTS, querying a idx_channel_pv_device built on 0067 (keyed by device + timestamp).

The original approach stuffed LANDED inside an aggregate FILTER:

count(DISTINCT c.device_id) FILTER (WHERE NOT c.is_bot AND {LANDED}) AS valid_devices

It looks natural enough—that’s exactly what FILTER is for. But EXISTS here is a correlated subquery, and the planner generates a SubPlan for it—meaning it runs once per real click. Over a 30-day window that’s 230,000 index probes, and this item alone accounts for 680 milliseconds.

The fix was to extract the whole “valid devices” concept into a standalone subquery, with LANDED written into its WHERE:

(SELECT count(DISTINCT c.device_id) FROM channel_click c  WHERE c.channel_code = $1 AND c.clicked_at >= $2 AND c.clicked_at < $3    AND NOT c.is_bot AND {LANDED})

Now the planner can see it: this is a semi-join between the click table and the landing table, hashable in one pass instead of 230,000 probes. That part goes from 680 ms → 300 ms.

The daily trend and per-channel list follow the same logic, rewritten as a single grouped subquery with LEFT JOIN. The caller of with_valid = false (the share page doesn’t show valid devices) saves even more—the subquery disappears entirely, replaced by a constant 0, without scanning the click table again.

But half the time is still there

After the semi-join rewrite, a large chunk of the remaining time is compilation overhead.

These SQL statements are sub-second OLTP queries; JIT is never worthwhile, yet the planner keeps triggering it by mistake. The reason is that the daily query uses generate_series left joins, and the row estimate comes out to about 200 million, far above the jit_above_cost threshold. A single JIT compilation takes 150–550 milliseconds, eating more than half of an already sub-second query.

So I added a read-only transaction to the stats endpoint:

async fn stats_tx(pool: &sqlx::PgPool) -> Result<sqlx::Transaction<'_, sqlx::Postgres>, AppError> {    let mut tx = pool.begin().await?;    sqlx::Executor::execute(        &mut *tx,        "SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY; SET LOCAL jit = off; SET LOCAL plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan",    ).await?;    Ok(tx)}

Three details:

  • A parameterless &str uses the simple query protocol, so all three statements go in one round trip.
  • I didn’t use sqlx::raw_sql—its execute would make the caller’s (the axum handler’s) future fail the Send check.
  • SET LOCAL only applies to this transaction and reverts once the connection returns to the pool; the transaction is read-only, so dropping (rolling back) at the end is enough.

The third directive was the most surprising

I didn’t initially think to add plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan.

Here’s the thing: sqlx caches prepared statements on the connection. After the same statement runs 5 times, Postgres switches to a generic plan—because a generic plan saves the 1–3 ms of replanning each time, a win for most high-frequency short queries.

But a generic plan can’t see the actual parameter values, hence not the window boundaries, so it estimates the time range as tiny. With the window estimated too small, the hash semi-join I’d just built degrades into a row-by-row nested loop. The funnel goes from 290 ms → 600 ms, twice as slow as before the fix, and it only starts being slow on the 6th request.

This isn’t visible to the naked eye. I wrote a throwaway test that ran the same batch of handler functions eight times in a row on the same connection to see the curve.

These endpoints aren’t hit often anyway, so an extra 1–3 ms of planning per call is negligible. So I forced a custom plan, always taking the measured hash semi-join.

How I proved the results didn’t change

Performance changes are the easiest way to accidentally alter semantics. This time I required byte-for-byte consistency, verifying two things:

  • The funnel row: compare md5 directly.
  • The md5 of the daily rows and the per-channel rows.

I verified both the 30-day and 7-day windows. Only when everything matched did I accept it.

Results (30-day window, benchmarked on the build machine):

EndpointBeforeAfter
Channel detail1.51 s0.64 s
Cross-channel overview1.49 s0.72 s
Share page0.85 s0.55 s

A few takeaways

A correlated subquery inside FILTER becomes a per-row SubPlan. As long as it can be extracted wholesale, extracting it is almost always the right call; FILTER is fine for cheap scalar checks, not for EXISTS.

"It’s faster after the change" isn’t necessarily true. This time, if I’d only looked at the first-run benchmark and not the curve after the 6th run, the conclusion would have been exactly the opposite. Slow queries in production often only show up after a connection has been reused for a while; a single benchmark won’t catch it.

JIT isn’t only enabled for big queries. It’s triggered by the estimated row count, and estimates can easily be pushed above the threshold by things like generate_series. Sub-second queries should just turn it off explicitly.

On top of stats_tx there’s also a coverage test: use a single-connection pool (only then is the connection fetched after the transaction ends guaranteed to be the same one, which is how you can tell whether SET LOCAL leaked into the pool), assert that all three settings really took effect inside the transaction, then try inserting a row in there and assert that it fails, and finally drop the transaction and re-run SHOW on the pool for jit and plan_cache_mode, which must be back to the default on / auto. If SET LOCAL leaks into the pool it contaminates every later query, which is far worse than being a bit slow.

These lessons now live in the function comments, right next to the code. If I’d written them in a blog post, three months later I wouldn’t be able to find them myself…
entry.summary: A statistics SQL query went from 1.5 seconds down to 0.64 seconds, at the cost of discovering that Postgres's generic plan and JIT each have their own timing.
entry.title: After Pulling EXISTS Out of the FILTER

entry.content:
In the opening comment of infra/migrations/0055_work_code_case_uniq.sql there’s a passage that was bought with a real production outage. Before I wrote it, I first wrote down a judgment — and production shot that judgment down…

Let me lay out the background first, otherwise that comment just reads like generic hand-wringing.

What we’re fixing isn’t “can’t find it”

0001_init.sql hands work.code a bare TEXT UNIQUE, i.e. UNIQUE (code), case-sensitive. But every read path on the site matches on lower(code) = lower($1).

The consequence of that mismatch isn’t “can’t find it” — it’s one title splitting into two rows in the database. In the 2026-08 batch the catalog pusher started sending the code as DASS-966 instead of dass-966; upsert_work's ON CONFLICT (code) didn’t match, so a new row got inserted. In production, three pairs actually split: DASS-966, DSOD-009, START-597 — merged by hand on 2026-08-29.

The symptoms after a split aren’t errors either; they’re two classes of silent failure:

  1. Half the data. The old row holds source_link, work_embedding, frame_embedding; the new row has only metadata. And ... WHERE lower(w.code)=lower($1) LIMIT 1 has no ORDER BY, so which row you get is up to the query plan. At the time, DSOD-009 and START-597 were getting the row with no play sources — the watch page returned 200 with not a single source.
  2. A flat 500. Any scalar subquery of the shape = (SELECT ... WHERE lower(code)=lower($1)) raises more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression when it hits multiple rows. Unfavorite, remove-from-playlist, and the similar-titles fallback all have that shape.

At the time, 0046_anime_import.sql:117-131 deliberately didn’t create the unique index right away, on the grounds that the existing dirty data would blow up the entire --single-transaction migration. Now that the data is merged clean, 0055 is here to tighten things up.

Why keep that case-sensitive constraint

What we’re creating is CREATE UNIQUE INDEX work_code_lower_key ON work (lower(code)). So can the old work_code_key (UNIQUE (code)) just be dropped along the way?

No. external_source_map.code is a foreign key pointing at work(code), and a foreign key requires a unique constraint on the referenced column, so DROP work_code_key would fail on dependency. And UNIQUE (lower(code)) is strictly stronger than it, so keeping it has no downside.

The non-unique functional index idx_work_lower_code created by 0046 can go, though — same columns, fully covered by the new unique index; keeping it just adds write amplification.

First judgment call: why it’s all wrapped in one DO block

Because LOCK TABLE only works inside a transaction block.

The production migration goes through psql --single-transaction in migrate.sh, which has a transaction block — no problem. But the local procedure recorded in tools/ugc-smoke/README.md is per-file psql -f, autocommit, no transaction block — a bare LOCK there just errors with LOCK TABLE can only be used in transaction blocks, and the local smoke DB ends up missing this unique constraint, which is the one and only thing this migration does.

A DO block carries its own implicit transaction, so it holds under both procedures. That also explains why LOCK and CREATE INDEX can’t be split into two statements.

Why grab the strongest lock right at the start

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX takes a SHARE lock, which blocks writes; DROP INDEX needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. Create-then-drop means a second lock upgrade inside the same transaction.

An online write that squeezes in between (the UPDATE work in increment_view) can’t get RowExclusive and queues; we then wait for it to yield; a cycle forms; deadlock detected; the whole migration rolls back. This was reproduced on the production database.

There’s an easy assumption to make: “nobody’s writing while the migration runs anyway.” It doesn’t hold: compose runs migrate to completion before it touches the api container, so during the migration the old api is still serving and increment_view keeps writing.

So one LOCK TABLE work IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE at the top grabs the strongest lock and never upgrades again — a cycle has no way to form.

Second judgment call: this is where I got it wrong

The first time this went to prd, lock_timeout was followed by “fail fast if the lock can’t be had.” The reasoning at the time: migrate exits non-zero, the api isn’t rebuilt, the old api keeps serving — so failing is the safe direction.

That judgment was wrong.

docker compose up -d does not preserve the old container just because migrate exited non-zero. It rebuilds api/web as usual; the new container just gets stuck at Created and won’t come up — depends_on: migrate: service_completed_successfully isn’t satisfied.

Net result: the migration didn’t take effect and the site went down outright. And the prd work table always has increment_view writing to it, so there was never any guarantee of grabbing ACCESS EXCLUSIVE within 15 seconds. An ordinary deploy took the site out.

The right approach is short timeout + repeated retries: wait only 2 seconds each round, let the queued write transactions finish, then try again. Online writes are all short transactions, so within a few rounds a window is bound to open. Only if 60 seconds pass without getting the lock do we RAISE — that means a long transaction is sitting on work, which calls for human intervention rather than forcing it.

FOR i IN 1..30 LOOP    BEGIN        PERFORM set_config('lock_timeout', '2s', true);        LOCK TABLE work IN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE MODE;        EXIT;    EXCEPTION WHEN lock_not_available THEN        IF i = 30 THEN            RAISE EXCEPTION '60 秒内拿不到 work 的 ACCESS EXCLUSIVE 锁（有长事务压着？先查 pg_stat_activity 再重试）';        END IF;        PERFORM pg_sleep(1);    END;END LOOP;PERFORM set_config('lock_timeout', '0', true);

A separate BEGIN/EXCEPTION per round creates an implicit savepoint, so a failed lock attempt rolls back only that round and doesn’t poison the whole migration transaction.

Error messages need to speak human

There’s one more gate before you create the unique index. If duplicates exist, it hands back a sentence you can act on directly, rather than a duplicate key value:

SELECT count(*), string_agg(lc, ', ' ORDER BY lc)  INTO dup, sample  FROM (SELECT lower(code) AS lc FROM work GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1 LIMIT 20) t;IF dup > 0 THEN    RAISE EXCEPTION      'work 存在 % 组大小写重复 code，须先人工合并（保留握有 source_link/向量的那行）再跑本迁移：%',      dup, sample;END IF;

“Keep the row that holds the source_link” has to be written in — reverse the merge direction and data is still lost, the unique index still gets built, and from then on that movie simply has no playback source.

Wrapping Up

EXECUTE 'DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_work_lower_code';EXECUTE 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS work_code_lower_key ON work (lower(code))';

Both go through EXECUTE: inside a DO block you could write the DDL directly, but the whole script uniformly uses EXECUTE to concatenate strings, tied together with the variables above so it reads as one thing from start to finish.

At the end of the migration file there’s also a ANALYZE work;, so the planner sees the new index as quickly as possible.

Looking back now, the file is 86 lines in total, and comments account for 52 of them. The longest passage is the record of that outage, reading “⚠️ This one was bought with production downtime”… Without it written down, the next person (or me three months later) will see “2 seconds × 30” and just think it’s verbose, then optimize it back to “fail fast.”
entry.summary: A misjudged "safe failure direction" took the whole site offline; notes on how a migration file's locking strategy was changed
entry.title: That One Comment Earned at the Cost of Production Downtime

entry.content:
A string of commits on the morning of August 4 had one theme: clearing sensitive values out of the blog config — the Baidu/Bing push tokens, the api_key used for LLM tagging, the passphrase for encrypted post categories — all moved into _config.local.yml of .gitignore, leaving only a _config.local.example.yml template in the repo.

Three related things happened the same day: the comment system moved from Twikoo+Waline to Artalk, the license changed from CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 to CC BY 4.0, and AI crawlers were let through with llms.txt generated. This post is about the cost of config layering, plus the GEO and attribution side of things.

De-sensitizing isn’t deleting the values

_config.yml is public, so writing a key into it is the same as publishing it. But a Hexo build still needs the real values, so the approach is layering:

# _config.local.example.yml（进仓库）hexo_submit_urls_to_search_engine:  baidu_token: ""  bing_token: ""llm_tagging:  api_key: ""encrypt:  categories:    - { name: 加密, password: "" }

Copy it to _config.local.yml and fill in the real values; the build deep-merges them with --config _config.yml,_config.local.yml. All four scripts — build / server / dev / push — have the merge arguments built in.

The upside is obvious: no real values in the repo, and the template tells the next person what to fill in. The downside is just as obvious: every command has to remember to carry that second config file, and forgetting it doesn’t throw an error — it degrades silently.

The two directions of forgetting

The first direction is a build that fails outright. After api_key was moved out of llm_tagging, _config.yml is left with only an empty parent key, and running hexo clean without --config throws an error on the empty config. So the hexo clean in clean and dev got the merge arguments too — even a command like “clean”, which looks unrelated to config, has to carry them.

The second direction is subtler: leave out the passphrase for encrypt.categories and the build won’t fail — posts in encrypted categories are simply output in plaintext. So there’s a warning line next to the encrypt block in _config.yml:

# ⚠ 不带 _config.local.yml 合并构建时，加密分类的文章会以明文输出

A config whose failure mode is “leak” is far more dangerous than one whose failure mode is “error”. The former needs someone to actively go look; the latter at least goes red.

The GEO part

Also that day: robots.txt now explicitly allows the major AI crawlers — GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and friends — and points at llms.txt and the two sitemaps; a new scripts/llms-txt.js was added, generating /llms.txt at build time.

The generator groups by first category, one - [标题](绝对URL): 摘要 line per post, and the summary strips code blocks, HTML and Markdown marks, truncated to 100 characters. Two edge cases are worth mentioning:

  • Encrypted posts are kept out of llms.txt so the summary can’t leak. After hexo-blog-encrypt processing, password is deleted from the post object, so the check has to re-read the frontmatter from the source file — the in-memory object can’t be trusted;
  • An individual post can opt out with llms: false in its front-matter.

On the sitemap side I tried hexo-generator-seo-friendly-sitemap's index-style splitting and rolled back to the official hexo-generator-sitemap two and a half minutes later: the site has only about 80 posts, so splitting into post/page/category/tag tables buys too little, and the official plugin is more actively maintained anyway. The llms.txt and robots changes stayed.

Attribution and license

Also that day, seven AI-drafted posts uniformly got copyright_author: Claude Opus 4.8 and copyright_author_href added, so the “article author” in the copyright box shows the collaborator instead of just me.

The license moved from CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 to CC BY 4.0: attribution, commercial use and derivatives allowed. I thought one thing through while making the change — a fair amount of what’s on the blog was already assembled from client-side corpora, official docs and material from all over, and the friction of the non-commercial restriction outweighed the benefit.

Wrapping up

After config layering, the public repo really is clean, but the system’s default state changed too: previously "just run hexo g" would build a correct site; now you have to remember the merge. Wiring it into every entry point only makes it the default, not automatic — anyone cloning the repo still has to cp the template and fill in values.

If someone asks again someday why the keys can’t just go back into _config.yml, the answer isn’t the word “insecure” — it’s: the public config and the buildable config are two different things from now on.
entry.summary: A record of sanitizing the configuration, llms.txt, and allowing AI crawlers — and how "a public config" and "a config that can build" are not the same thing
entry.title: After moving the secret key out of _config.yml, every command has to remember to include the other config file

entry.content:
The Butterfly release notes for the jump from 5.6.1 to 5.7.0 state one thing plainly: built-in APlayer/Meting support has been removed. After upgrading, the aplayerInject config stopped working, and the related entries in layout/includes/third-party/aplayer.pug and plugins.yml vanished along with it.

/music/ holds 188 <meting-js>, and inject also contains one fixed player. The tags themselves are still there, but the script injection is gone, so the page just shows a row of empty custom elements.

At this point the story should be “the upgrade broke the players, so roll back or hand-write the inject.” But I measured the baseline first, and the result was a little surprising.

Before the upgrade, it was already zero

meting-js defaults to MetingJS’s built-in backend api.i-meto.com. That service is already dead: its responses carry no CORS headers, so every browser request fails. In other words, not a single player on the live site had been rendering for a while — nobody had just bothered to count.

The theme upgrade isn’t the culprit; it merely pried up a floorboard that had rotted long ago. That distinction matters: roll back the version and the page returns to a state where “the player code looks like it’s there, but the count is still zero,” and you keep assuming it’s fine.

Hand-writing the inject: order is a hard constraint

The fix is to include them yourself, in order, inside inject:

<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://registry.npmmirror.com/aplayer/latest/files/dist/APlayer.min.css" media="print" onload="this.media='all'">...<script src="https://registry.npmmirror.com/aplayer/latest/files/dist/APlayer.min.js"></script><script>window.meting_api="https://meting-api.saop.cc/api?server=:server&type=:type&id=:id&r=:r"</script><script src="https://registry.npmmirror.com/meting/latest/files/dist/Meting.min.js"></script>

window.meting_api must be set before Meting.min.js; one line later and it has no effect. For CSS, use media="print" + onload to switch to all, which doesn’t block first paint.

The pjax glue script was actually dead code

The theme also used to have a pjax hook that destroyed and rebuilt destroyAplayer on page switches. Looking into APlayer 1.10.1, window.aplayers is no longer maintained, so that destroyAplayer had nothing to destroy in the first place.

MetingJS v2, meanwhile, is a standard custom element, so on page switches it rebuilds and destroys itself via connectedCallback / disconnectedCallback. So the conclusion this time is no glue: let the element own its own lifecycle.

After fixing it, count

Measured after the change:

  • players rendered: 0 → 167/188;
  • after a pjax round trip, every in-page player is rebuilt;
  • the fixed player stays the same DOM node throughout, with playback uninterrupted.

Of the remaining 21, twenty are type="album" — the self-hosted Meting API doesn’t support that type yet and returns 400. The other one or two are intermittent failures caused by rate limiting under 188 concurrent requests. Both are on the API server side and unrelated to this repo; the commit message says as much, and I didn’t count them as “fixed.”

167/188 isn’t a perfect score, but it’s a number you can re-check: render count, pjax round trip, and fixed-node identity each have their own observation point.

When upgrading, separate the two accounts first

The most expensive part of a dependency upgrade isn’t editing config; it’s being able to say clearly, before the upgrade, what things actually look like right now. This time the baseline was a single sentence — zero — and it decided every judgment that followed:

  • if the zero had been caused by the upgrade, I should suspect the 5.7.0 changes, or even roll back;
  • if the zero was an old debt and the upgrade merely made it visible, I should fix the backend and the injection order, not roll back.

Along the way I also cleared out a piece of dead code. Had I been lazy and copied destroyAplayer verbatim into the new inject, it would have “worked” too — it would just do something useless against an empty array on every page switch, and the next person would have even less chance of seeing why it exists.

Measure what things looked like before, then decide what the upgrade broke.
entry.summary: After Butterfly 5.7 removed APlayer support, fixing from 0 to 167, and the fact that the default backend had long been out of service
entry.title: 188 Players, 0 That Play Sound: An Old Bug Exposed by a Theme Upgrade

entry.content:
There’s a page on the site called /masturbation that publicly shows each day’s count and an annual heatmap, plus an admin backend /dash/masturbation where the administrator can backfill, edit, and clear entries. The data is private and the page is ordinary: a year-scoped query RPC, a calendar, a date input and a count input.

On launch day there was a bug that silently ate data.

0 means both “nothing that day” and “zero out that day”

The heatmap loads by year, and the editor’s selectedCount comes from the current year’s query result. On the 2025 page, the admin changes the date to 2024-03-12—

  • The date in the input changes, but the page still holds 2025 data;
  • selectedCount can’t find that day in the 2025 array and falls back to 0;
  • The count input shows 0;
  • Click save, and 0 is written.

If 2024-03-12 originally had 7 recorded, that one “nothing was changed” save wipes it out. Here 0 is both the display default for “no record” and the write value for “clear the record” — the two look exactly alike.

Let the date carry its own year

The first instinct might be to add a hint: “switch the year first for cross-year dates.” But the more reliable fix is to make the year part of the selection state:

  • Selecting a date that doesn’t belong to the current year immediately navigate('?year=2024&date=2024-03-12');
  • The loader loads that year’s data based on the year param, and brings the initial selected value back in via the date param;
  • The route component uses year:initialDate as the key, so the whole editor remounts when crossing years;
  • Until the new data arrives, the save button is disabled.

The key guard is this line:

const unavailable =  busy || navigation.state !== 'idle' || Number(selected.slice(0, 4)) !== year

As long as the selected year differs from the current page’s year, saving isn’t allowed. That way, even if navigation is slow and the user is fast, the 0 from “last year hasn’t been read back yet” never gets written.

After a successful save, instead of refetching the whole year, update the local days with the returned value: if the count is greater than 0, replace or insert; if it’s 0, remove it from the array. The old useQuery + invalidateQueries are gone too, saving a round trip and removing the need to maintain the retry branch for when the query.isError refresh fails.

The heatmap itself isn’t that mysterious

The calendar lays out cells using UTC dates: from January 1 of the year back to that week’s Sunday, then day by day forward past January 1 of the next year and filled out to a full week. The page has 365 or 366 buttons, future dates are disabled, and counts only take rows from <= today. Month labels compute the column number from which week the 1st of each month lands in; the annual total, days recorded, and single-day maximum are all derived from the counts.

today uses Intl.DateTimeFormat to pin Asia/Shanghai, so it doesn’t read the server process timezone. Both /masturbation and the admin send Cache-Control: no-store, so an anonymous user clicking save gets a 401.

Links between the public page and the admin, the previous year’s ←, and the next year’s → are all there; the year is only allowed from 1970 through the current year, illegal years get a 400 and no fake records are generated. The initial table is just empty — no sample data is stuffed in.

Phone width

The same round also fixed overflow in the admin at 390×844: outer flex-wrap, date input min-w-0 max-w-full, stat cards changed from a fixed three columns to repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 100px), 1fr)), year heading whitespace-nowrap. The e2e asserts documentElement.scrollWidth <= innerWidth.

The heatmap itself allows horizontal scrolling on narrow screens, but only inside the chart — it doesn’t stretch the whole page.

How to nail down the regression

The new e2e first saves 2024-03-12 as 7, then opens the 2025 admin, fills in this cross-year date, asserts that the count input becomes 7 within 1.5 seconds, clicks save, and finally checks the year endpoint that it’s still 7. In finally it writes the original value back, so other cases aren’t polluted.

The other case only does the phone-width check. Neither relies on “the user remembering to switch the year first.”

Wrapping up

The implicit primary key of a time-series form is (year, day). Choosing across years isn’t changing a string — it’s switching the data source; treating “loading” as a disable condition is more reliable than any hint.

Fields like 0, which are both a value and a default, are most dangerous when they get submitted as the “current value” before the data has arrived. Read it back first, then allow writes.
entry.summary: Public daily counts and a yearly heatmap, and what is easiest to overwrite when 0 is both a value and the default
entry.title: The Year-Rollover Trap of a Date Input: Read the Year Back Before Saving

entry.content:
On September 29 and 30, twenty-one commits over two days moved nav-site from Vercel + Neon to a Singapore VPS: Cloudflare Tunnel in, the origin exposes no public ports, postgres binds only to 127.0.0.1:5432, the app runs in Docker Compose, and builds are done on the server with a dedicated buildx builder.

The migration ultimately succeeded. But those earlier commits were almost all patching the same category of thing: assumptions the platform used to make on my behalf. This post records them in order of discovery, not in commit order.

One hop lands on 0.0.0.0:3000

Before switching production, I tested in preview: the 302 landing point for /r/<渠道码> was https://0.0.0.0:3000/, and the same applied to the callback redirects after successful and failed Google login. If the redirect entry point had only been discovered on production switch day, every short link on the site would have broken at once.

The root cause is in attachRequestMeta of next-server.js: in standalone mode, next-server holds the hostname/port it listens on and prioritizes them when constructing the request URL, so the experimental.trustHostHeader branch is never reached. On Vercel, the platform automatically trusts Host (config.js is enabled at hasNextSupport), so this was never exposed before the migration. In testing, neither Host nor X-Forwarded-Host affected req.url; only the protocol followed X-Forwarded-Proto.

The fix is a newly added lib/public-origin.ts: take the Host header (the origin is reachable only through the tunnel, and Cloudflare writes Host based on the domain the visitor requested), and for the protocol accept only https from X-Forwarded-Proto. Deliberately do not trust X-Forwarded-Host—visitors can supply it themselves, Cloudflare passes it through unchanged, and trusting it is an open redirect.

I also replaced openapi.json and llms.txt along the way: they used to prioritize reading XFH to build the site root, which is forgeable after self-hosting, and the endpoint is cached at the edge for an hour, which amounts to cache poisoning.

Same commit, prod and preview fight over one image tag

Both sides build nav-site:<sha>. But the same commit does not produce identical artifacts on both sides: the database connected at build time, prerendered data, and NEXT_PUBLIC_* can all differ. Whichever builds later takes over the tag—in testing, when production built later, the preview container’s image became an unnamed sha256:…; conversely, a production restart or rollback would end up on a build containing preview data.

Changed to nav-site:<env>-<sha>, so build, release, rollback, and cleanup all carry an environment prefix. Image identity cannot rely on commit alone; things with different artifacts should not share one name.

Secrets don’t enter the cache key

When releasing via CI on the VPS for the first time, between two commits only the deploy/ script changed (it does not enter the build context), and the whole pipeline hit cache and completed in 5 seconds. The cache itself was not the problem, but it exposed a quieter hazard: build-time environment variables are injected via BuildKit secrets, and the secret contents do not participate in the cache key. When only env changes and the code does not, pnpm build hits the old cache and the new NEXT_PUBLIC_* silently fails to take effect.

The fix is that deploy.sh passes the first 16 characters of the build env file’s sha256 as a build arg, and echo it in Dockerfile. As soon as env changes, the cache is invalidated.

EXIT trap references a local variable; a successful release exits 1

The EXIT trap in cmd_build_deploy / cmd_migrate used a function-local variable. The trap only fires when the script exits after the function returns normally; under set -u it reports “unbound”, turning a successful release into exit code 1—CI then marks every success red. After cleanup completes, trap - EXIT is removed.

pg-verify treats “empty vs. empty” as a match

When running the import against Neon for the first time, the source database failed to connect because of a certificate parameter. Yet pg-verify output “✓ sequence values match”—both sides were empty results, and since the table loop was empty there was no ✗ either. Although the script ultimately exited non-zero because of set -e, it reached no clear conclusion; on the night of the switch, it could easily have been read as a pass.

Now it first confirms both ends are reachable and that the source database really has tables under public; otherwise it exits 2 immediately. One more note: for libpq with sslmode=verify-full, sslrootcert=system must be added; Node’s pg driver does not recognize this parameter, so the connection string used by the app should contain only sslmode=verify-full.

Backups in a public bucket

The original recommendation was to create a new private backup bucket; later we decided to use the primary bucket nav-bucket directly—it has a public CDN domain attached, is publicly readable, and its object keys contain timestamps that make them guessable. The database contains user emails, password hashes, and partner keys; uploading it in plaintext would be equivalent to making it public.

So everything is age-encrypted before upload; if BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT is empty, the upload is refused outright (fail-closed), and ciphertext is placed under a prefix with a random suffix. The decryption private key is in /opt/nav-site/env/backup-age.key; a separate copy must be stored outside the machine: if the machine is lost entirely, the backups on R2 can only be decrypted with it.

Splitting one key into three

CHANNEL_REPORT_SECRET, USER_SESSION_SECRET, ADMIN_SESSION_SECRET, and CRON_SECRET all used to fall back to the same value, so the validity of externally shared links ended up tied to a key whose name gave no hint of the connection. When we split them apart during the migration, deploy.sh refuses to publish if any one of them is missing.

Among them, changing CHANNEL_REPORT_SECRET invalidates every externally shared link and QR code already sent to partners, so it must be stored somewhere other than the server; the others can be rotated at any time, and the only cost is that whoever happens to be logging in fails once. Keys that can be rotated at any time and keys that can’t must not look the same.

A few more that look harmless but bite

  • fail2ban on this machine bans you for 24 hours after 3 authentication failures. When you can’t connect, find out why first — don’t go guessing usernames.
  • sshd has port forwarding disabled, so migrations, script runs, and database queries all happen on the server itself; there is no SSH tunnel to fall back on.
  • The migrator keeps no record table. It reruns everything by filename every time, so migration files must be idempotent.
  • A deploy normally takes about 7 seconds with zero failed requests, and a bad version that won’t start is rolled back automatically. But Docker’s service-name resolution ignores health status: a version that can listen on the port yet returns wrong responses will receive roughly half the traffic during the health-check window, which lasts up to 30 seconds. That boundary is written into the runbook; we didn’t pretend it doesn’t exist.
  • Run a restore drill at least once a quarter — a backup that has never been restored isn’t a backup.

The defaults after the move

Vercel trusted the Host for you, gave every build its own identity, guaranteed that your backup bucket was private, and said “consistent” for you when a result was empty. Self-hosting doesn’t make these things disappear; it turns them from the platform’s defaults into your own defaults: one publicOrigin, one <env>-<sha> label, one sha256 build arg, two preflight checks, and one age public key.

What really matters in a migration checklist is never the commands — it’s whether each of these assumptions has been caught, one by one.
entry.summary: Two nights during a VPS self-hosting migration: 0.0.0.0 redirects, image tags, BuildKit cache, empty-to-empty validation, and public bucket backups
entry.title: After Moving Off Vercel, the Safety Nets the Platform Provided Started Showing One by One

entry.content:
In September’s auth milestone, email OTP, password reset, and Google login all wrapped up together. Among the things the first review round turned up, one was related to rate limiting, and I’m writing it down because it’s nothing like “just configuring a few numbers.”

Look at the code order first

better-auth’s email-otp plugin first calls resolveOTP (email-otp/routes.mjs:31) in the endpoint, unconditionally inserting a code row; the sendVerificationOTP callback that sends the email only runs after that. On consumption, consumeVerificationValue (internal-adapter.mjs:818-860) only ever recognizes “the latest row for that identifier,” and on consumption it deleteMany all rows.

The old code hung the rate-limit check inside the send-email callback, i.e. after that insert. Once it tripped:

  1. resolveOTP had already written a new code row;
  2. The callback checked the rate limit, refused to send, and that row never reached anyone’s inbox;
  3. The user entered the old code from the email in hand; it matched the latest row, and INVALID_OTP;
  4. Both rows were wiped together.

The user was stuck: the code in their inbox was dead, no new code could be obtained within the cooldown window, and the error message said “invalid code,” putting the blame on the user.

Move it before the insert

The fix is to block at hooks.before. The dispatch supports a before hook returning an object without the context key to short-circuit (the end of runBeforeHooks + else if (before) in dispatchAuthEndpoint), the endpoint handler doesn’t run at all, and that row never gets written.

All three invariants were kept, each with its own assertion:

  • The rate-limited response is byte-for-byte identical to the “email not registered” response (status code + body + content-type all compared);
  • Rate-limited requests send no email;
  • The first request in the window still sends exactly one email. With the check running before the insert, the old -1 compensation in assertOtpRateExcludingCurrent was deleted too.

The rate-limit layer itself turns into a registration oracle

The second version’s problem was subtler. resolveOTP leaves a persistent verification row for a registered email, but better-auth immediately deletes the just-inserted row for an unregistered email (enumeration defense — both request-password-reset and forget-password/email-otp do this). If a rate-limit hit threw 429, then hammering the same address twice would directly tell an attacker whether that email has an account, depending on whether the status code sequence was (200,429) or (200,200).

Before the identifier format was fixed, the counter was mute — it neither protected nor leaked; after the fix, the counter actually started counting registered emails for the first time, and the side effect became observable.

PathOn rate-limit hitRationale
Password resetSilently skip sending, endpoint still returns 200“Rate-limited” and “email doesn’t exist” must be indistinguishable
Email verification429The sign-up endpoint already leaks the same fact once via USER_ALREADY_EXISTS_USE_ANOTHER_EMAIL, and /verify's resend button needs real feedback

One footnote to this table: whoever one day plugs the sign-up leak must at the same time change the email-verification 429 to a silent short-circuit, otherwise it’s only half plugged.

Rejected requests must not leave a row

The hourly quota counts rows in the verification table. In the old implementation, rejected requests also left a row, so an attacker could fill a victim’s quota with five straight hits — only one email actually went out, but the person was locked out for an hour.

With the check moved before resolveOTP, rejections leave no row. There’s a dedicated regression case:

expect(await countOtpRows('forget-password', email)).toBe(1)

Reverting would count to 2. What the quota should count is “emails actually sent.”

Rescuing a one-shot path

The same round also had the squatting arbitration. When Google login hits an unverified email, it deletes the squatter’s password in databaseHooks.account.create.after. The function had only been reasoned through for “a crash between the two deletes,” never for “any throw anywhere in the function body”:

create.after → queueAfterTransactionHook (with-hooks.mjs:33 didn’t give onError, re-throws as-is) → createWithHooks → linkAccount → generic catch, returns unable to link account. And the account row is already committed; a throw can’t undo it.

The user sees one login failure, retries → takes the already-linked branch (link-account.mjs 135–181); that branch doesn’t trigger the hook but does set emailVerified to true. Endgame: the email is verified, the victim logged in with Google, the squatter’s password still works as usual, and it’s indistinguishable in hindsight — it looks exactly like “an already-verified account hooked up to Google.”

The fix is to wrap the whole function body in try/catch, swallow it, don’t rethrow, and just log a single [auth] 抢注仲裁失败 … entry with the userId. The reason for not rethrowing is written in the comment: throwing can’t undo the already-committed link, it only adds one more inexplicable login failure, and the retry takes the branch that doesn’t even log, which buries the hole deeper. The test mocks db.transaction to make it throw, asserting the return is false, the log has the userId, and the password is still there.

“Please verify your email first” needs to actually be clickable

Someone else in the same round hit another one: they registered, closed the tab, came back the next day to post, and got stopped by a 403 saying “Please verify your email before posting content.” — a dead end with nothing clickable in it, and site-wide /verify only links out from the registration page and the Google button. Even if you found /verify, the page opens by announcing “a verification code has been sent to your email,” but that page never sends a code on load — the line is a lie.

We changed email_unverified to render as "copy + a link to /verify", across eight user-side render points. The copy in /verify became “Enter the 6-digit code you received… if it didn’t arrive, hit the button below to request one”, updated in all three languages; the resend button moved from ghost to outline. No auto-send on page entry — that would burn the per-email hourly quota on every refresh.

An Empty String Is Not “Not Configured”

There’s another of the same kind on the deployment side. The docs say in four places that “omitting the email variables doesn’t error, it just behaves wrong; if MAIL_TRANSPORT isn’t passed it defaults to console.” That’s false: Compose substitutes host variables that were never set with an empty string, and ?? 'console' and .default() only accept undefined; parseMailEnv({ MAIL_TRANSPORT: '' }) throws outright, and the symptom is that the api container won’t start.

Crashing is the better behavior, so we didn’t grant empty strings an exemption — instead we wrote the contract down clearly: this group of variables must exist and be non-empty, and if the container won’t start, check the email config first. Two assertions in mail/config.test.ts pin it down.

The test and e2e scripts, meanwhile, hard-prefix MAIL_TRANSPORT=console. Shell environment variables take precedence over --env-file, so without that prefix, once you’ve set MAIL_TRANSPORT to resend locally: a single test run fires off a batch of real emails to actual inboxes, and e2e fails outright because it can’t read the verification code from stdout.

Wrapping Up

Rate limiting isn’t a set of numbers, it’s a position in the write order. Get the position wrong and what it stops isn’t the attacker — it’s the email in the user’s hands.
